Below are some suggestions:

+*Clause 3.1*+

We could:

* Limit scope to direct breaches: Propose indemnity only for direct breaches of law or gross negligence by your company.
* Exclude third-party actions: Clarify that indemnity does not cover actions by independent drivers or third parties outside your control.
* Carve-out for force majeure or unforeseeable events.

+Proposed Clause Revision:+

“The service provider shall indemnify the client solely for direct losses resulting from proven breaches of applicable transport regulations or gross negligence by the service provider.”

+*Clause 3.2*+

We could:

* Shift responsibility to the contractor: State that drivers are subject to national regulatory standards, which your company ensures through selection and monitoring, not direct supervision.
* Limit obligations to “reasonable efforts” or “contractual covenants with providers.”

+Proposed Clause:+

“The service provider shall ensure, through contractual arrangements with its transport partners, that drivers meet regulatory and safety standards. The service provider shall not be considered the employer of individual drivers.”

+*Clauses 3.9 – 3.12*+

We could:

* Request flexibility in branding and operational methods.
* Replace mandatory standards with “reasonable commercial efforts.”
* Avoid fixed vehicle specs unless required by law or safety.

+Proposed Clause:+

“The service provider will use reasonable efforts to ensure vehicles used meet the agreed standards, and will consult the client before implementing material operational or branding changes.”

+*Section 15*+

Wouldn’t uncapped indemnities  and responsibility for third-party regulatory breaches that we can’t control be viewed as inequitable or unenforceable anyway, especially if we're not the direct operator?

We could:

* Introduce a liability cap (e.g. 100% of annual contract value).
* Exclude indirect/consequential losses (like business disruptions).
* Limit responsibility to direct breaches by your company.

+Proposed revision:+

“The total liability of the service provider shall not exceed (X amount), excluding cases of wilful misconduct or gross negligence. Indirect or consequential damages are expressly excluded.”

----

+*Section 16*+

For insurance, the law does not mandate operators hold insurance for others, unless they directly provide the service..

We may have to:

* Clarify we don’t directly operate vehicles.
* Offer to require insurance from subcontractors and confirm it contractually.
* Remove requirement to notify of insurance changes unless we are the policyholder.

+We can propose:+

“The service provider will ensure that transport partners maintain legally required insurance coverage and will make certificates available upon reasonable request.”

Our request to only be liable for direct breaches or negligence and to require insurance from subcontractors would be aligned with commercial norms and Czech practice.

+*Section 18*+

We could offer to:

* Cap penalties and tie them to actual damages.
* Allow limited publicity with prior approval (e.g. anonymized case studies).

+Proposed Clause:+

“Breach of confidentiality shall be subject to a penalty capped at CZK (some reasonable amount), unless actual damage is proven. Public reference to the client may be made with prior written consent.”

+*Clause 20.3*+

+We can propose:+

“The service provider shall make available training materials provided by the client to relevant personnel and use reasonable efforts to ensure their review. Additional training requirements will be agreed with reasonable notice.”

*Section 21*

This imposes very high penalties, which may not be enforceable in full under Czech Civil Code (Act No. 89/2012 Coll.)

We can propose capping penalties and linking them to actual damage is supported by Czech contract law principles of fairness and proportionality.

+We can propose:+

“Penalties shall not exceed CZK (monthly cap), and shall be payable within 30 days of notice. Delays of less than 10 minutes shall not trigger penalties unless systemic. The service provider shall have the opportunity to explain or dispute any penalty before it becomes payable.”

Mr [~accountid:6130627ef0bf520069526076] made me these magic boots that fit over the caliper to measure the width of the guide channel 🙏 

!image-20250805-100432.png|width=724,height=965,alt="image-20250805-100432.png"!



Measurements were all taken in the middle of the battery, near the gasket. On C2 I used the rear cap top part for reference point. 

Results:

C2 battery: 140.80mm

Erkis NG Jig: 141.35mm

C3 without corepack: 141.25~141.35mm _*three different casings measured slightly differently_

C3 with corepack: {color:#ff5630}141.60mm{color}

C3 with sanded corepack: {color:#ff5630}141.40mm{color}

Heavily worn test-battery (standard C3 with corepack inside, dots not sanded) from Riga: ~141.25mm *(wear is uneven, slight adjustment along the battery can give different result. Some areas near the bottom of the battery are as low as 140.90mm)*

*Conclusion:*

* From these measurements it is clear that the side channel width exceeds our required tolerance. 
* With sanded down corepack injection dots we can reduce the width of the battery by 0.2~0.3mm. *I think that this step should be added to the SOP.* Just need to think of a way how to do it efficiently and without damaging the battery. I used narrow belt sander and it worked well. 



Also, when using the magic boot as a comparison jig, it can easily be noted that the side channel on the heavily worn battery is considerably wider and the jig has a play in the channel while the unused C3 casing fits the jig snugly. I believe this play in the side channel combined with slightly worn down guide bottom surface is why this battery does not stick in the frames. If this kind of modification can be made to the mold, it would help solving this issue. 

I will discuss with [~accountid:6130627ef0bf520069526076] how to measure out the amount of wear on the worn-in battery from Riga and whether this can be implemented in the mold.

# *Session cookie:* We ask for the user’s phone number, then we send an OTP code, and the user is logged-in. As this is a web page, *it creates a session authentication cookie. This cookie should last only for the session* (once the order is made and some time thereafter to be able to submit a ticket to the CS) and then *the user should be logged out because we cannot extend the session cookie longer than necessary for the session.* This cookie is a necessary cookie, so we don't need the user's consent for this. But if we don't log out the user, this cookie requires a consent (simple "Remember me") is enough.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Legal explanation of point 3:*
{panel}

Art 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive states that "*the storing of information,* or the gaining of access to information already stored, *in the terminal equipment of a user* is only *allowed on condition that the user concerned has given his or her consent". However, there are 2 exemptions from the user's consent, one of which is when this storage is*{{ strictly necessary to provide the service explicitly requested by the subscriber or user. }}

Without the use of an authentication token/similar thing stored in a user's device, the user would have to provide a phone number and OTP code on each page request. Therefore this authentication functionality is an essential part of the service that is explicitly requested by the user. All cookies or other things that require storage of authentication information on user's device are under this rule. As Bolt can rely on the exemption described above, we should not store this authentication token/similar thing longer than for a session (make an order, deliver the order, and some time thereafter to be able to submit a ticket to the CS). *It means, once the user closes a page (in case no order is made) and when the order is delivered and the user closes a page, we should log out the user from the web app. Otherwise, we need a consent as described above as we will fall outside the exemption.*

‼️ *We have three options:*

* *Log out the user* once the user closes a page (in case no order is made) and when the ride is completed and some time thereafter (30-60 mins max).
* *Implement "Remember me" checkbox*, so it's recognized as consent to store this info longer than permitted by the exemption. However, we should have a clear purpose for storing this session cookie longer than for a session (aka ride).
* As OTPs are expensive, we may *accept the risk* as we have done for Food Web App and proceed without log-out. The risk is medium for such a violation.

*Notes from EC FAQ:* [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-frequently-asked-questions-about-data-act|https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-frequently-asked-questions-about-data-act|smart-link] 

*16) Can there be multiple users for a single connected product, and how should their access be governed?* 

Various actors may have a legal right based on the contractual arrangements related to the use of a connected product. It is therefore entirely possible for multiple persons to be users of the same connected product. In such a situation, data holders should have mechanisms in place to ensure that each user can access the data to which they are entitled. Users might also conclude separate agreements (e.g. a userto-user sub-lease of a connected product). 

The following example illustrates, in a non-exhaustive manner, how access to data in a multiple-user scenario could be organised. Other data-sharing arrangements and mechanisms are possible. The Commission's upcoming model contractual clauses will provide further guidance (cf. Question 71).

Example: Sara goes on holiday to Portugal for 2 weeks and needs to rent a car. The rental agency, Sunny Wheels, owns a fleet of cars bought from Omni Motors, a large car manufacturer. Keen to exercise her rights under the Data Act, Sara asks Sunny Wheels to provide her with a 'connected car'. 

Sunny Wheels has a contract with Omni Motors that ensures that Sunny Wheels and its clients can access the data generated by the car. Omni Motors has put in place a data management system that can simultaneously handle data access requests from the thousands of users of their cars.

Sara's rental agreement contains detailed information on the data generated by the car, including how to access it. The following are two possible ways of organising access to data generated by Sara's rented car.

'Corporate accounts': Sunny Wheels has a corporate account with Omni Motors. Sunny Wheels provides Sara with the details needed to log in to Omni Motors' website and access the rented car's data. 

'Individual accounts': Sunny Wheels informs Sara that she has to set up her own account and enter into a separate data-sharing contract with Omni Motors. Sunny Wheels notifies Omni Motors that Sara will be using the car for 2 weeks. 

In both cases, Omni Motors is the data holder; Sunny Wheels is a user because it owns the rented car and can access the data; and Sara is also a user because she has, by virtue of the rental agreement with Sunny Wheels, received temporary rights over the rented car.

*21) Is a manufacturer always a data holder?* 

Even though manufacturers will typically be data holders, this is not always the case. The Data Act allows an entity to 'outsource' the role of 'data holder'. For example, a manufacturer may contract out to another entity the role of 'data holder' for all or part of the manufacturer's connected products. 

In addition, a data holder who is not a manufacturer might be a company that provides a related service linked to a connected product This means that the business offering the related service might be a data holder and be different from the company that actually made the connected product. 

Determining who the data holder is does not depend on who produced the hardware or software, but on who controls access to the readily available data. See the flowchart below for an example of role distribution.

*23) Does the new data access right affect the protection of trade secrets?* 

The Data Act provides a framework that balances data sharing with the need to preserve the protected nature of the data (including with respect to the protection of trade secrets, whose confidentiality continues to be ensured). The Data Act does not modify the applicable legal protections (including the 2016 Trade Secrets Directive, which already provides a legal framework for the protection of trade secrets). 

However, a data holder can unilaterally determine which data are trade secrets, so the claim that certain data are trade secrets is not enough to prevent the exercise of the data access rights provided by the Data Act. This does not mean that the Data Act leads to the forfeiture of trade secret protection. Rather, it carefully balances the need to prevent illegitimate restrictions on the user's new data access rights against the need to uphold the legal protection provided to trade secrets. 

The data holder therefore has the right, prior to disclosure, to require users and third parties to preserve the confidentiality and secrecy of the trade secret encumbered data by agreeing to and implementing safeguards necessary to that end. As an additional layer of protection, the Data Act introduces a new mechanism (commonly known as the 'trade secrets handbrake') that frames the conditions under which a data holder can withhold, suspend or, exceptionally, refuse to share data.

*Notes from EC Data Act explained:* [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/data-act-explained|https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/data-act-explained|smart-link] 

h2. Chapter II: Business-to-business and business-to-consumer data sharing in the context of the IoT market

h3. _Why?_

A key objective of the Data Act is to *create fairness in the data economy* and *empower users* to reap value from the data they generate using the connected products that they own, rent or lease.

The Data Act enables users of *connected products* (e.g. connected cars, medical and fitness devices, industrial or agricultural machinery) and *related services* (i.e. anything that would make a connected product behave in a specific manner, such as an app to adjust the brightness of lights, or to regulate the temperature of a fridge) to access the data that they co-create by using the connected products/ related services.

The availability of such data will significantly impact the economy. For example, data generated by connected products and related services can be used to boost aftermarket and ancillary services as well as to create entirely new services, benefiting both businesses and consumers. 

h3. _Types of data in scope_

Chapter II of the Data Act on business-to-business and business-to-consumer data sharing applies to *all raw and pre-processed data generated from the use of a connected product or a related service that is readily available to the data holder* (e.g. manufacturer of a connected product/ provider of a related service), in other words data that can be easily accessed without disproportionate effort, going beyond a simple operation. This applies to both personal and non-personal data, including relevant metadata.

Such data includes data collected from a single sensor or a connected group of sensors, such as temperature, pressure, flow rate, audio, pH value, liquid level, position, acceleration or speed.

Inferred or derived data and content (e.g. highly enriched data, audiovisual material) are out of scope. Furthermore, the Data Act is without prejudice to the laws on the protection of [+intellectual property rights+|https://commission.europa.eu/business-economy-euro/doing-business-eu/intellectual-property-rights_en].

_For example, if a user watches a film on their connected TV, the film itself is not within scope but data on the brightness of the screen is within scope._

h3. _In practice_

Chapter II of the Data Act allows *users* (i.e. any legal or natural person who owns, rents or leases a connected product) to access the data that they generate through their use of the connected product or related service. If the user wishes to share this data with another entity or individual (‘*third party*’), they can either do so directly or they can ask the data holder to share it with a third party of their choice (excluding gatekeepers under the [+Digital Markets Act+|https://digital-markets-act.ec.europa.eu/legislation_en]). The *data holder* is typically the company that makes the connected product or that provides a related service. A data holder must have a contract with the user (e.g. sales contract, rental contract, related service contract, etc.) defining the rights regarding the access, use and sharing of the data that is generated by the connected product or related service. It is important to note that the data holder cannot use any non-personal data generated by the product without the user’s agreement.

By way of example, and bearing in mind that the relevant contract determines the exact roles:

* _A company operates a bulldozer: the data holder would typically be the bulldozer manufacturer, and the user would be the company that operates the bulldozer._  
* _If someone buys a connected fridge and downloads an app that helps them to regulate the optimal temperature for the content of the fridge, there would potentially be two data holders, namely the entity that placed the fridge on the market and the entity offering the related service (the app), and only the one user (the owner of the fridge)._

The Data Act incudes several mechanisms to make it easier for users to be able to make use of these provisions: data holders must provide the user with information on the type of data that they will generate when using the connected product or related service (including the volume, collection frequency, etc.); users should be able to request access to the data through a simple process, and; data holders must make the data available to users for free.

Hi [~accountid:5d428d25d9cd0e0da3a1b03e] 

h3. 2c2p Refund Statistics *(05 July– 05 August 2025)*

Based on the data available in ProcessOut:

* *234 refund attempts* were made.
* *56 refunds* were successfully processed.
* *175 refunds* failed with the error:
“2c2p returned a transaction response code error: 12: Transaction status is not valid to perform your action.”
* *3 refunds* failed with the error:
“The gateway timed out.”

This means *75% of 2c2p refunds are currently failing.*

*Example payment:*
[Payment link|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3533981949]
These refunds fail with a *PERMANENT ERROR* message and are not retried automatically.

----

h3. Financial Impact

The monthly financial impact is relatively low. However, this contradicts the Payments team’s motto:

{quote}_“We don’t mess with customers’ money.”_{quote}

Current financial impact: *34,087.69 THB (≈ 911.12 EUR)*

----

h3. Alternative Solutions

[~accountid:5b612cc5e859072d9083d40a] suggested introducing a retry mechanism for refunds after 24 hours, instead of delaying them.

----

h3. Should We Stop Routing Payments to 2c2p?

We also explored the option of routing payments through dLocal instead of 2c2p.

* Current routing split: *24.2% via 2c2p* and *75.8% via dLocal*.
* dLocal’s pricing is very similar to 2c2p’s. According to [~accountid:5b612cc5e859072d9083d40a] , dLocal might even be slightly cheaper (this needs to be confirmed).

That said, there is value in maintaining multiple PSPs in Thailand, as they can serve as fallbacks for each other.
However, it’s worth noting that *dLocal uses 2c2p services internally to some extent* (exact details unknown).

----

h3. How Are Refund Issues Currently Resolved?

Refund issues are only fixed when CS escalates the case to Payment OPS via the Commerce Service Desk.
OPS then manually processes the refund using the 2c2p portal.

----

h3. Why Don’t We Have the Same Issue with MB Way Anymore?

Refund issues with MB Way were resolved after switching to the {{/refund}} API endpoint:

* [Jira Ticket|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/PC-4102]
* [Slack Thread|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/GE93NHVTP/p1707895127892169]

However, in April 2025, a new issue was introduced: *MB Way only supports a single partial refund per payment.*
Since this change, *110 refunds have failed* because CS teams attempted to process multiple refunds for the same payment.

h3. 🔍 Summary: Bolt Guardian AZ – Slack Thread (Week of 29 July – 5 August)

h4. 📌 1. *Legal Advice Summary*

* *CCTV* is mandatory in taxis in Azerbaijan (Decree #183), providing a *lawful basis to record without consent* for certain legal/state purposes only.
* *Consent is required* for Bolt Guardian features such as:
** Live customer support monitoring
** Trip sharing and alerts
** Rider/booker access to footage
** Proactive interventions
** Any business-purpose data use

*Consequences for non-compliance*:

* Fines up to 20,000 AZN (~£9,000)
* Criminal liability (Article 156.1)

h4. 📲 2. *Consent UX Flow*

* Local legal advice requires *explicit consent via an in-app screen*.
* *Screen must include*:
** Clear legal wording
** A button (e.g. “I accept” / “Continue”) that must be clicked to proceed
** *Interaction logging* for audit/regulatory evidence

*Consensus:*

* Button will likely be labelled *"Continue"* (used elsewhere in Bolt).
* Consent screen to be shown:
** *Once per user* for the *Pilot*
** Possibly more frequently for full launch (e.g. per ride or per profile)
* *Critical* that the user *cannot bypass* consent by closing the screen.

h4. 🧪 3. *Pilot Phase Plan*

* Duration: *3 months*
* Coverage: *200 vehicles*
* For the pilot:
** Consent functionality may not be logged yet
** Logging must be implemented *before full launch*
** Simpler consent text might be used temporarily (discussed as Option 1)

h4. 🚗 4. *In-Vehicle Signage*

* Required to notify *third-party passengers* (who don't consent via the app).
* Must include:
** *Visible CCTV signage*
** *QR code* linking to Bolt’s Privacy Notice
* Fleet partners to implement signage as standard.
* Local Ops (Sakina) requested a *timeline for final mockups* (Azerbaijani language)

h4. 🛠 5. *Technical & Implementation Status*

* @Dash and @Veronika collaborated on UX wording (Google Doc circulated).
* @Shivam.atri will lead consent feature implementation.
* *Product (Ernesto)* confirmed:
** Implementation not started
** Must be raised formally as a *new dependency* for prioritisation
* Pending confirmation from Product whether button interaction can be tracked

h4. 📋 6. *Outstanding Tasks*

* Finalise wording/content for consent screen (by *end of week*)
* Confirm mechanics of consent screen (timing, blocking booking, tracking)
* Finalise signage mockups and print plan
* Confirm data system registration with local authorities

Thanks for flagging the proposed Relocation Feature. 

Kindly could you clarify the purpose or need behind requesting the old fleet’s approval during a driver relocation: 

* Is this step intended as a control mechanism, or purely administrative (e.g. confirming offboarding tasks)?
* What happens if the old fleet refuses – is this intended to prevent the relocation, delay it, or simply log a concern?

From a French Labour law perspective, the rationale behind this step is important, as granting a veto to the old fleet could conflict with the driver’s right to seek new employment. This right cannot be overridden by another employer’s refusal, unless the employment contract contains specific and lawful restrictions, which is rarely the case in fleet models.

From a data protection perspective, transferring personal data between fleets – who are likely independent controllers – triggers several GDPR obligations:

* The driver must be informed clearly and in advance of the data transfer, its purpose, the new recipient (fleet), and their rights.
* A valid legal basis for processing must be established. Legitimate interest may apply, but this must be documented and balanced via a legitimate interest assessment (LIA).
* Data minimisation principles apply strictly – only necessary, up-to-date, and relevant data should be copied.

To this, I would like to add some additional questions: 

* do you know the scope of what is being copy pasted to the new fleet? 
* Are all past warnings, suspensions or terminations linked to the driver’s account being transferred from one flete to another?

Hi [~accountid:5d9c300987dd6f0dcb4d2b58] 

*T&Cs*

* I’m currently updating the principal terms, which should be finalised by 1 August. The new version will allow us to contract directly with fleets that are set up as limited companies.
* This is already possible under the agency model in the UK, though as I understand, there are currently no plans to launch fleets under that model here.

*Offline Addendums* 

* On fleet onboarding, while the updated T&Cs will be in place from 1 August, we may still want to put in place offline agreements with some fleets to cover things like incentives or additional commercial terms.
* For example, with Bolt Lux fleets, we created a specific template that sets out quality requirements - we might need something similar depending on how we structure any future fleet partnerships.

*Existing 1 Fleet* 

* Also worth flagging that we already have one fleet in London - Odyssee. They were onboarded via an offline agreement that effectively varied our existing T&Cs to allow contracting with a limited company. Given that they operate under a different incentive model compared to our standard Bolt Link drivers, from a product perspective they should be treated as a proper fleet, not as a Bolt Link Driver A.

*Bolt Boost / Reclassification Risk / Increased Financial Exposure* 

* Removing Bolt Boost increases our financial exposure. If a fleet driver later brings a claim for worker status, we could be liable for unpaid benefits if incentives like Bolt Boost were not provided. 
* The fleet structure helps mitigate this risk, particularly where drivers are employed by the fleet, *but it’s not bulletproof.* It ultimately comes down to whether we’re seen as exercising indirect control or whether there’s a strong enough economic dependency on Bolt.

To reduce this risk, we should:

* Avoid any direct enforcement actions against fleet drivers
* Encourage or allow multi-apping

One concern is the Ops team's proposal to enforce a minimum acceptance rate at fleet level. Even if it’s not applied at the individual driver level, the pressure may still trickle down, increasing the perception that we’re indirectly controlling driver behaviour. If Bolt Boost is removed and these types of controls are introduced, we risk unintentionally increasing WS exposure.

My suggestion is that we carry out a risk assessment that looks at:

* The impact of removing Bolt Boost from fleets,
versus
* The WS risk if we introduce all these additional product and operational features (e.g. acceptance rates, onboarding flows, quality checks etc)

This will help us understand the combined risk profile and whether we need to soften or adjust our approach, or accept a slightly higher risk but manage it properly with the right safeguards.

Hey! We can’t just create an invoice, but rather we should do it through manual adjustments, because we also need to adjust the balance. I recommend the manual adjustment “deduction_commission” as it will appear on the provider’s weekly report as well as invoice (thus creating the missing invoice). 

However, the other aspect is that if we do the deduction in one part, it might mean that the provider’s balance goes negative for some time while they recoup the commission adjustment amount. 

I checked an it seems like their average weekly sales is around 2000czk, so either you can make an adjustment for the whole amount of 16238.09 and then it would take them around 8 weeks before they receive a payout again or adjust in portions (e.g 1500czk every week until 16238.09 is reached). Whatever the provider prefers. The second option is obviously a bit more annoying, as it would need to be done every week. 

Regarding other restaurants with similar problems, I’m already looking into this and have created a ticket to the owning team to review how this tag is used and if we can somehow either restrict it or make the naming more clear. Notification to data subjects is governed by *Section 22 of the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA)*. It states that where there are _reasonable grounds to believe_ that personal information has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorised party, the responsible party must notify both:

# The *Information Regulator*, and
# The *data subject*, subject to limited exceptions.

Since our investigation confirms that unauthorised access occurred to Fleet Managers’ accounts, we have reasonable grounds to conclude that their personal data—and potentially that of associated data subjects—was compromised. Therefore, notification to *both Fleet Managers and affected drivers* is legally required.

Hello, 

The debt comes from this order [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/2069592182/307?orderTryId=2551300627|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/2069592182/307?orderTryId=2551300627].

The customer used and APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancel it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the ned of the ride, the order price decrease, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since service was provided, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineers are currently working on sending the right refund amount for these cases where a partial refund was previously made automatically. 
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance to compensate for the debt in their account or a refund to their payment method on a different order?

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

From a tax perspective, both *intermediary* as well as *resale models* can be launched in Canada, Ontario :green_circle: .

It should be noted that:

* Bolt should issue invoices to business customers in its own name for the re-supply of transportation services and is not merely acting as an agent for the drivers. 

* If it is clear that Bolt is liable to pay the drivers, then Bolt will be considered the recipient of the supply and will generally be able to claim input tax credits (“ITCs”) for any HST payable. If the Business customer is liable to pay Bolt, then the Business customer should be able to claim ITCs based on the invoice from Bolt so long as it is using the services in its commercial activities (i.e. it would be able to claim an ITC in the same manner as if the drivers invoiced them directly)

For the tax treatment of coupons, some additional clarifications are still needed from the local advisors.

Hi [~accountid:712020:cb6fc720-3c42-4171-99dd-eaefef0e51eb], 

Thanks for flagging the proposed Relocation Feature. 

Kindly could you clarify the purpose or need behind requesting the old fleet’s approval during a driver relocation: 

* Is this step intended as a control mechanism, or purely administrative (e.g. confirming offboarding tasks)?
* In which circumstance would an Old fleet refuse a transfer? Are there any criteria to enable that refusal, if yes, are those described? (e.g. exclusivity?) 
* What happens if the old fleet refuses – is this intended to prevent the relocation, delay it, or simply log a concern?

From a French Labour law perspective, the rationale behind this step is important, as granting a veto to the old fleet could conflict with the driver’s right to seek new employment. This right cannot be overridden by another employer’s refusal, unless the employment contract contains specific and lawful restrictions, which is rarely the case in fleet models.

From a data protection perspective, transferring personal data between fleets – who are likely independent controllers – triggers several GDPR obligations:

* The driver must be informed clearly and in advance of the data transfer, its purpose, the new recipient (fleet), and their rights and they must accept the transfer of their data. They cannot just be informed, they need to acknowledge and accept this transfer.
* A valid legal basis for processing must be established. Legitimate interest may apply, but this must be documented and balanced via a legitimate interest assessment (LIA).
* Data minimisation principles apply strictly – only necessary, up-to-date, and relevant data should be copied.

To this, I would like to add some additional questions: 

* do you know the scope of what is being copy pasted to the new fleet? 
* Are all past warnings, suspensions or terminations linked to the driver’s account being transferred from one flete to another? 

Thank you !

Hi all, to clarify briefly, from a SK VAT perspective, if we have a netting mechanism, it means the branding bonus is not consideration paid in exchange for a separate taxable supply or as remuneration for the provision of transportation services, but rather is a commission rebate. 

*Analysis*

Bolt charges a commission (Bolt Fee) in exchange for providing the bundle of Bolt Services. This bundle of services includes the provision of the Bolt Platform, which is a software-as-a-service in that the driver is granted a license to use the Bolt Platform to generate leads for passenger transportation. The Bolt Fee is paid based on the amount of the fare for each completed passenger transportation service provided by the driver using the Bolt Platform.

The driver T&Cs do not specifically address the branding bonus and the branding bonus does not seem to fall within a campaign that guarantees a minimum income. However the separate branding terms do address the branding bonus. The branding terms define “Service” as the driver undertaking to provide (1) transportation services (2) with the driver’s vehicle with the Bolt branding, (3) in the prescribed minimum number and time, and (4) all in accordance with the branding terms. The terms further state that the Services are provided free of charge, and only after fulfilling and complying with the applicable driver T&Cs are drivers entitled to apply for the branding bonus. As a result, the branding bonus is a conditional incentive, not a guaranteed service fee, and only available after meeting specific criteria when carrying out the passenger transportation service. The driver voluntarily participates in the branding program by signing up via a form and any compensation is optional and performance-based. From a VAT perspective, since a supply without consideration is not a taxable supply and is outside the scope of VAT, the branding T&Cs do not seem to create a separate economic activity carried on by the driver.

In sum, the Bolt fee is a commission calculated as a percentage of each trip fare and paid in exchange for using lead generating software. From a VAT perspective, the driver is not providing a distinct advertising service under the branding terms (such as licensing the right for Bolt to put advertising on their vehicle). The branding bonus is performance-based and directly reduces the net economic burden of the Bolt Fee. Because the branding bonus functions economically as a discount or incentive applied to the commission, it reduces the driver’s effective cost of using the platform and functions as commission rebate; it is not a guaranteed minimum campaign or similar where Bolt is subsidizing part of the price of the transportation service. Thus, from a tax perspective, where the netting mechanism is applied, we do not view the branding bonus as a separate taxable supply or as remuneration for the provision of transportation services.

*Risk*

In terms of tax risk under the netting mechanism, our local counsel has advised that there is 80% chance of success if the arrangement was challenged in court. The risk initially is on the driver and only if they are not a VAT-payer. In SK, drivers that aren’t VAT-payers because their annual turnover is below the minimum threshold for registration are nonetheless taxable persons and must identify themselves as such. That means because there is a cross-border supply of the Bolt SaaS, the reverse charge mechanism applies since the driver is a taxable person, but the driver must instead register as an identified person and self-assess the input VAT paid the commission. If the commission is reduced by a branding bonus, then there is risk that the driver has underpaid SK VAT. While this risk technically lies with the driver, Bolt could be held responsible for not properly calculating the commission taxable amount and would have to issue corrected tax invoices. 

*Recommendation*

If our intent is to treat the branding as a separate taxable supply, then the branding terms could be redrafted to reflect that by explicitly framing the bonus as consideration paid to the driver in exchange for granting Bolt a license to use their vehicle for brand display. Otherwise, to support our current tax position, it may be more effective to consolidate the bonus mechanism within the Driver T&Cs (e.g., Section 9), and explicitly state that the branding bonus functions as a rebate reducing the Bolt Fee taxable amount. We would also need to ensure the commission invoices clearly reflects the reduced commission and resulting VAT base.

Hi [~accountid:5f0c30effe23000022252e68]!

Our opinion is that *everything has to work in-app*, which means that:

a) *either the person is already registered on the app and uses the kiosk only to log in to their existing account*, with the kiosk functioning only as a device different from their phone;

b) o*r the person is not subscribed and will have to do so (sign up on the app)*, providing the same data and information they would provide if they were subscribing to the app on their phone.

*In either case, it is important that everything works as if it were in-app, applying all the rules, such as the minimum age of the passenger, price information, etc*. (everything that is mandatory to provide, in accordance with Article 19 of the TVDE Law). It must also be possible to send the invoice to the customer (Article 15/8 of the TVDE Law).

We also note that the TVDE Law expressly states that _“Payment for the service is processed and recorded through the electronic platform, and payment is only permitted through electronic means”_ (Article 15/7), so we would like to point out in advance that *cash payments cannot be requested.*

Given that the *Law provides for payment by electronic means*, we do not believe there is any problem with payment via ATM or QR Code, provided that this is *done through the platform.*

Our T&Cs for passengers state that in-app payment corresponds to _“bank card, mobile device payment, and other means of payment used by the Passenger to pay for Transportation Services through the Bolt App,”_ so I believe it would not be necessary to change them.

For *privacy reasons*, we believe it is essential to have a *mechanism in place to ensure that the customer logs out before the next customer places their order.* This is because it is natural for people to forget to log out, in which case their personal data will be exposed and vulnerable to third parties.

Furthermore, as [~accountid:712020:011a9eb3-77af-4c62-bb26-e6c10e6097ec]  mentioned, authorizations/licenses/contracts will depend on where you intend to install these kiosks.

[~accountid:5ac11e86b1d07b580252a584] UK real estate law is significantly more complex and risk-laden than in many other jurisdictions - not sure if your team are aware of that or taken that into consideration. Unlike in Germany or other EU countries, there is no standardised lease form, and much of the legal risk is contractual and location-specific. This includes:

* *Potential title or ownership issues*, which we cannot ascertain without external counsel;
* *Extensive tenant (repair) obligations*, even under short-term leases;
* *Environmental and compliance risks*, particularly if liability is not clearly limited in the lease – including (but not limited to) the fact that the warehouse has an asbestos roof, which raises additional health, safety, and liability concerns; and
* *No confirmation of planning permission*, which may render our intended use unlawful.

In this case, the draft lease provided doesn’t reflect a short-term 9-month arrangement – it reads more like a long-term institutional lease (because Dott have copy and pasted their 5 year lease and are trying to shift all of the responsibility onto Bolt!). We also haven’t been given essential supporting documents and we’re dealing with counterparties who are not UK real estate specialists, which makes resolution of key points slower and more difficult.

It’s also worth noting that while the annual rent figure is €200k, the total financial exposure could significantly exceed that if the lease makes us responsible for repairs to the building, roof, or structural elements, or if we were found liable for asbestos remediation or environmental damage on the site.

So while the headline value may seem modest, the legal and operational risk is disproportionate if not properly addressed.

The input I’m seeking from external counsel is not a luxury or a nice-to-have – *it’s the bare minimum required to avoid exposing Bolt to disproportionate risk* for a relatively modest commercial arrangement.

Thank you for your detailed feedback on the process. I appreciate you raising this point, and I completely agree that we should avoid any potential confusion or expectation gap for employees. 

For us, the Confluence page is crucial for three main reasons:

# *Formal Documentation:* It's the official record for policy and system changes, which is vital for historical context and future reference.
# *Cross-Team Alignment:* It's a central place for all stakeholders (Accounting, ERP, People, Tax teams) to align on the final details and formally sign off on the plan.
# *Governance:* It provides a clear audit trail of what was approved and when, which is essential for compliance.

However, I agree with you that releasing this information to the public before it's live in Workday creates a challenge.

We suggest creating a restricted internal section in Confluence as our source of truth for all requirements. Then, once the implementation is complete and a go-live date is set, we would copy the finalized information to a public Confluence page. This would still uphold the importance of Confluence as our source of truth but would perfectly sync the public announcement with the live change.

Jira as a tool should not be the place where we keep the requirements, but to track projects. 

What are your thoughts on this approach?

When we took on the first Driver Hub in London (before my time), we signed a long lease at around £40k per month. We didn’t conduct a full condition survey before signing, and as a result, ended up spending €1.5 million replacing the roof and €700k on installing a new air-circulation system. The previous tenant had left the building in a poor state, but the landlord refused to cover any of these costs – and they were fully entitled to do so, because under the lease, those obligations sat with us.

That outcome was avoidable. But it happened because the business moved ahead without understanding the legal and technical risks attached to the property. This is exactly the type of exposure I’m trying to prevent.

To be clear: Legal cannot sign off on the current warehouse lease in its present state. Without proper due diligence, Bolt is being asked to take on potentially significant legal, financial, and operational risk — and that’s not something we can endorse.

# How we can prevent fraud best in your market in this scenario? 
## Pre-authorising/Booking whenever we can the first hour/predicted payment to ensure a working payment method: _depends on user payment method_

# How we can limit fraud?

### The right to limit access to this category for those not ‘qualifying’ due to fraud suspicion
